Spatial analysis for cities: transport accessibility, population and public services.

I combine OpenStreetMap, population grids and satellite imagery to find where people lack access to transport and services, and turn the results into clear maps and recommendations. I work in QGIS (network analysis, PyQGIS scripting) and ArcMap, and script my workflows so they can be re-run when the data are updated.

Independent project · October–November 2026

Who can walk to a bus stop? Transport accessibility of Nura district, Astana

Nura is the fastest-growing district of Astana: 188.5 km² and about 251,000 residents. I found where homes, schools, clinics and shops are too far from public transport, ranked those places, and tested where new bus stops would help most.

64,600residents (26%) live more than an 800 m walk from a bus stop
57%of facilities are within a 400 m walk of a stop (80% by straight line)
34% · 19%of schools and kindergartens have a stop within a 400 m walk
+36,400residents brought within 800 m of a stop by 14 proposed stops

Data

  • OpenStreetMap (October 2026): district boundary, 201 bus stops, 156 facilities in 9 categories, 2,330 km of walkable streets.
  • WorldPop 2025, 100 m constrained population grid.
  • All layers in EPSG:32642 (UTM 42N), stored in one GeoPackage.

Method

  1. Walking catchments of 400 m and 800 m from every stop along the street network (QGIS Service area).
  2. A 100 m grid (19,224 cells) with access class, built-up flag and population for each cell.
  3. Walking distance from each facility to the nearest stop: multi-source Dijkstra in PyQGIS.
  4. Priority index = weighted facility demand within 800 m × lack of stop access; underserved zones of at least 0.1 km².
  5. Greedy placement of 14 new stops (at least 500 m apart) and recalculation of coverage for area and residents.

Key findings

One resident in four lives more than a 10-minute walk from any stop. The largest gap is the south-western housing area (zone No. 1: 4.5 km², about 29,800 residents). Real walking routes are on average 1.6 times longer than the straight line: blocks, fences and missing crossings raise the average distance to a stop from 288 m to 447 m. Schools and kindergartens are the worst-served facilities, and these are the trips children and parents make every day.

Scenario

Fourteen new stops raise the share of residents within 800 m of a stop from 74.2% to 88.7%, and the built-up area within 800 m from 68.0% to 83.7%. Most of the gain is in zone No. 1 (about 27,600 residents).

How much of the district is covered?

BaseWithin 400 m400–800 mOver 800 m
Built-up area (about 49 km²)49.0%19.0%32.0% (15.8 km²)
Residents (about 250,800)55.4% (139,000)18.8% (47,200)25.8% (64,600)
Whole district (188.5 km²)12.7%5.2%82.1%

Most of the district is undeveloped steppe, so the built-up area and the number of residents are the fair bases for comparison.

Priority zones and recommendations

Built-up cells with no stop within 800 m form 17 zones covering 13.2 km². A zone's total score grows with its area, so I added the score per km² to separate “large” zones from “intense” ones.

  • First: new stops in zone No. 1, which has the largest total need.
  • Separately: a stop for zone No. 4. It is small, but its score per km² is about three times that of zone No. 1, and none of the 14 proposed stops reaches it.
  • Central cluster C: the 121 highest-priority cells fall outside every zone because they lie in the 400–800 m band. They need infill stops 300–400 m apart on streets that already have routes.
  • Check school and kindergarten access in any revision of the route network.

What I learned

  • Straight-line distance hid a large part of the problem: along real streets, schools and kindergartens turned out to be the worst-served facilities.
  • An index summed over zones rewards size. Dividing by area changed the ranking and brought a small, intense zone (No. 4) to the top.
  • Zones built from a single threshold can hide the most important places. Checking where the index is highest revealed the central cluster that the first scenario missed.
  • Adding population turned “square kilometres” into “people”, which is what planners and residents actually care about.

Limitations: the study measures distance to stops, not routes, frequency or travel time (GTFS data would allow time-based accessibility). Results depend on how completely OpenStreetMap maps footpaths, and WorldPop is a modelled estimate that may lag behind new housing.

How the walking distance was computed (PyQGIS)

director = QgsVectorLayerDirector(walk_network, -1, "", "", "", QgsVectorLayerDirector.DirectionBoth)
director.addStrategy(QgsNetworkDistanceStrategy())
builder = QgsGraphBuilder(crs, True, 10)            # 10 m snapping tolerance
tied = director.makeGraph(builder, stop_points + facility_points)
graph = builder.graph()
S = graph.addVertex(stop_points[0])                 # virtual source linked to every stop
for i, p in enumerate(stop_points):
    graph.addEdge(S, graph.findVertex(tied[i]), [p.distance(tied[i])])
tree, cost = QgsGraphAnalyzer.dijkstra(graph, S, 0)  # one run gives distance to the nearest stop
